blocks.text: Information gain measures how much a decision tree learns by splitting a dataset on a particular feature, computed directly from the entropy covered in the first lesson of this module. It is the exact criterion greedy decision tree algorithms use to decide which feature to split on at every single step.

blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together

blocks.text: 1. What Information Gain Measures

Information gain answers a specific question: if a dataset is split into groups based on a feature value, how much does the entropy, the class-label uncertainty, drop as a result. A feature that produces groups where one class clearly dominates gives high information gain, while a feature that leaves each group just as mixed as before gives close to zero.

This is exactly the same greedy question a good game of 20 questions asks, which single question narrows down the possibilities the most, information gain answers that same question mathematically for a dataset split.

A feature can only ever have zero or positive information gain, never negative, since the conditional entropy lesson from the entropy topic already established that learning extra information can never increase uncertainty.

A feature that leaves the label distribution completely unchanged after splitting on it produces exactly zero information gain, correctly signaling it carries no useful predictive signal at that particular node.
2. The Formula

Information gain is defined as IG = parent entropy minus the weighted average of the child entropies, where each child weight is the fraction of the total data points that ended up in that child group.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: If a parent group has entropy 1.0 and splitting produces two children with a weighted average entropy of 0.4, the information gain is exactly 0.6, meaning the split removed 60 percent of the original uncertainty about the label.

blocks.text: This formula generalizes cleanly to splits with more than two child groups, simply weight and sum the entropy of every resulting child, not just a left and a right one.

Both the parent and child entropies in this formula are computed with the exact same entropy function introduced in the first lesson of this module, nothing new needs to be learned mathematically, only how the pieces fit together.
3. A Worked Split Example
Consider a dataset of 8 examples with labels [yes, yes, yes, yes, no, no, no, no], split by a feature into a left group [yes, yes, yes, no] and a right group [yes, no, no, no].

code.content:
parent = ["yes","yes","yes","yes","no","no","no","no"]
left = ["yes","yes","yes","no"]
right = ["yes","no","no","no"]
print(information_gain(parent, left, right))

blocks.content: {"headers":["Group","Labels","Entropy"],"rows":[["Parent","4 yes, 4 no","1.0 bit, maximum uncertainty"],["Left","3 yes, 1 no","about 0.811 bits"],["Right","1 yes, 3 no","about 0.811 bits"]]}

blocks.text: Since both children still carry meaningful entropy, this particular split only partially resolves the uncertainty, leaving room for a decision tree to keep splitting further down each branch.
Running the code above confirms the information gain for this particular split lands around 0.189 bits, a modest but genuinely positive reduction in uncertainty.
Notice the two child groups happen to share the exact same entropy value here purely by coincidence of the numbers chosen, that will not generally be the case for an arbitrary split on real data.
4. Choosing the Best Split

A decision tree algorithm computes information gain for every candidate feature, and every possible split point for continuous features, then picks whichever split produces the highest information gain at each node. This greedy, one-step-at-a-time strategy is what ID3 and C4.5, two classic decision tree algorithms, use to build a tree.

This greedy, one-node-at-a-time strategy never looks ahead to consider whether a different, locally worse split might lead to a better overall tree several levels down, which is a known limitation of decision trees compared to more exhaustive search methods.

This process repeats recursively at every new child node, treating each one as its own smaller dataset needing its own best split, until a stopping condition like maximum depth or minimum group size is reached.

This exhaustive per-feature comparison is exactly why training a decision tree on a dataset with many features and many unique values can take noticeably longer than training on a smaller, cleaner one.
5. A Perfectly Pure Split

The best possible information gain occurs when a split produces perfectly pure child groups, each containing only one class label, driving child entropy all the way down to 0 and recovering the entire parent entropy as pure gain.

code.content:
pure_left = ["yes","yes","yes","yes"]
pure_right = ["no","no","no","no"]
print(information_gain(parent, pure_left, pure_right))   # 1.0, the maximum possible gain here

blocks.text: A perfectly pure split like this is rare on real, noisy data, most useful splits fall somewhere between zero gain and this theoretical maximum, still meaningfully reducing uncertainty without fully resolving it in one step.

This maximum-gain case corresponds directly to a leaf node in a decision tree, once a group is fully pure there is no more uncertainty left to reduce, and that branch of the tree can safely stop growing.
Achieving this maximum in a single split requires a feature that already perfectly aligns with the label, an ideal, rarely occurring case worth recognizing when it does happen.
6. Information Gain and Overfitting

A feature with many unique values, like a customer ID, can produce an artificially high information gain simply by creating many tiny, pure groups, one per unique value, without capturing any genuinely useful pattern. This is a well known weakness of raw information gain, addressed by a related measure called gain ratio, which penalizes features with excessively many possible values.

A tree that keeps splitting on high-cardinality identifier-like columns tends to memorize training data rather than learn a genuinely useful pattern, exactly the overfitting risk that limiting tree depth or using gain ratio helps guard against.
Removing obviously identifier-like columns before training, or applying gain ratio instead of raw information gain, are two standard, complementary defenses against this specific bias.

Cross-validating a decision tree, rather than trusting a single training split, is a broader safeguard against overfitting worth pairing with the gain-ratio fix, catching cases the entropy criterion alone might miss.
7. Information Gain in Feature Selection

Beyond building trees, information gain, often called mutual information in this broader context, is used directly to rank and select the most informative features for any model, not just decision trees, by measuring how much each feature alone reduces uncertainty about the target label.

code.content:
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif
scores = mutual_info_classif(X, y)
print(scores)   # higher scores mean more informative features

blocks.text: This feature-ranking use case is exactly the mutual information idea introduced in the KL divergence lesson applied concretely, ranking every candidate feature by how much it alone reduces uncertainty about the label.

Ranking features this way before training any model at all is a fast, model-agnostic first pass at understanding which raw inputs are likely to matter most, well before committing to a specific algorithm.
Combining this feature ranking with domain knowledge, rather than trusting the numeric score blindly, usually produces the most reliable feature set for a final model.
8. Gain Ratio: Fixing the Many-Values Bias

Gain ratio corrects the many-unique-values bias covered in section 6 by dividing information gain by a term called split information, which measures how many pieces a feature splits the data into and how evenly. A feature that splits data into many tiny groups gets a large split information penalty, bringing its gain ratio back down closer to features that split more sensibly.

C4.5, the successor to the original ID3 decision tree algorithm, switched to gain ratio specifically to address the identifier-column bias covered in section 6, making it a more robust default in practice.

A feature with only two roughly equal-sized groups gets a modest split information penalty, while a feature splitting into dozens of tiny groups gets a much steeper one, exactly targeting the bias raw information gain suffers from.
9. Information Gain Versus Gini Impurity

Gini impurity is a related but distinct measure of how mixed a group of labels is, computed differently from entropy but capturing a similar underlying idea. Some decision tree implementations, including scikit-learn default, use Gini impurity reduction instead of information gain, since it is slightly cheaper to compute and tends to produce very similar trees in practice.

code.content:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
model_entropy = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion="entropy")   # uses information gain
model_gini = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion="gini")           # uses Gini impurity reduction

blocks.text: Both measures peak at the same maximally mixed 50/50 point and both reach zero at a perfectly pure group, the specific numeric values differ slightly, but the resulting choice of best split is very often identical or nearly so.

Entropy involves a logarithm, making it very slightly more computationally expensive than Gini impurity, which only involves squaring, a small but real reason some large scale implementations default to Gini for speed.
10. Information Gain for Continuous Features

For a continuous, numeric feature, information gain is computed by first sorting the data by that feature, then testing candidate split thresholds between consecutive distinct values and computing information gain for each candidate split, keeping whichever threshold produces the highest gain.

code.content:
sorted_vals = sorted(set(feature_values))
candidate_thresholds = [(sorted_vals[i] + sorted_vals[i+1]) / 2 for i in range(len(sorted_vals)-1)]
# information gain is computed for each threshold, then the best one is kept

blocks.text: Testing every midpoint between consecutive sorted values guarantees the optimal threshold is found, since the best possible split point for entropy reduction always lies exactly between two data points, never in the middle of a large empty gap.

This threshold search is more computationally expensive than the categorical feature case, since it requires testing many candidate splits rather than one, which is part of why decision tree training time grows with the number of continuous features and unique values.
11. A Worked Example
A dataset of 10 emails is labeled spam or not spam, and a feature indicates whether the email contains the word free. Compute the information gain of splitting on this feature.

code.content:
parent = ["spam"]*6 + ["not_spam"]*4
contains_free = ["spam"]*5 + ["not_spam"]*1   # 6 emails contain the word
no_free = ["spam"]*1 + ["not_spam"]*3         # 4 emails do not
print(information_gain(parent, contains_free, no_free))

blocks.text: This spam-detection example is a realistic, small scale version of exactly the kind of split real spam classifiers built on decision trees actually rely on, individual words or phrases acting as strong signals for one class or the other.
A real spam filter would repeat this exact calculation for hundreds of candidate words, keeping only the ones with the highest information gain as the first few splits in the tree.
12. Common Mistakes

items: Preferring a feature purely because it produces a high information gain without checking for the many-unique-values bias covered in section 6.
Computing information gain on a very small sample, where entropy estimates are noisy and unreliable, and small groups can misleadingly appear pure by chance.
Confusing information gain with information itself, gain measures a reduction, a difference between two entropy values, not an absolute quantity.
Forgetting to weight child entropy by group size, an unweighted average would incorrectly let a tiny group influence the result as much as a large one.

blocks.text: A related trap worth naming directly: assuming a feature with 0 information gain is always useless, it may still combine usefully with other features even though it carries no predictive signal entirely on its own.

Always sanity check a suspiciously high information gain against the number of unique values the feature has, a near-perfect split on a column that is nearly unique per row is usually a red flag rather than a genuinely useful pattern.
13. Practice: Compute Information Gain
A dataset has labels [yes, yes, no, no, no] and a feature splits it into left [yes, no] and right [yes, no, no]. Compute the information gain.

code.content:
parent = ["yes","yes","no","no","no"]
left = ["yes","no"]
right = ["yes","no","no"]
print(information_gain(parent, left, right))

blocks.text: Compare the resulting gain against the perfectly pure split example from section 5, this smaller value reflects a split that only partially, not completely, resolves the original label uncertainty.

Try computing the entropy of the parent, left, and right groups individually before combining them, confirming by hand that the weighted subtraction matches whatever the information_gain function returns.
Key Takeaway

Gain ratio, from section 8, and Gini impurity, from section 9, are the two most common practical refinements applied on top of raw information gain, worth recognizing by name when reading decision tree library documentation or research papers.

Information gain measures how much a feature split reduces entropy, computed as parent entropy minus the weighted average entropy of the resulting child groups. It is the exact criterion greedy decision tree algorithms use to pick the best feature to split on at every step, and it generalizes into mutual information based feature selection for any model.

This lesson closes the loop on the pure information theory ideas covered in this module, entropy measures uncertainty, cross-entropy and KL divergence measure mismatch between distributions, and information gain applies those same ideas directly to the concrete, practical task of building a decision tree one split at a time.

Whether building a tree from scratch for a class assignment or reading through a random forest documented split criterion, the same underlying idea keeps reappearing, reduce uncertainty about the label as much as possible with each decision made.
